title: 12,700 Indian Tech Professionals Returned From the US in Nine Months, Nearing the 2025 Record
excerpt: Xpheno estimates put returns at 84 percent of last year's record by September, as suspended PERM processing, layoffs and visa uncertainty push mid-career professionals toward India.
body:
• About 12,700 Indian white-collar technology professionals moved from the United States to India between January and September 2026, according to staffing firm Xpheno's estimates reported by The Economic Times — 84 percent of 2025's full-year record of 15,100, reached in just nine months.
  • Returns have climbed steadily: 7,200 in 2023, 9,800 in 2024 and 15,100 in 2025, putting 2026 on course to set another record.
  • The drivers are visa-policy uncertainty under the Trump administration, sustained tech layoffs, and suspended PERM green-card processing at major employers including Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Tata.
  • Returning is not an automatic soft landing: Indian employers are prioritising AI, cloud, cybersecurity and product-leadership skills over overseas experience, and returnees face tax-compliance obligations in both countries.

Reverse migration on the India–US tech corridor has reached a scale that would have been hard to imagine five years ago. Roughly 12,700 Indian technology professionals left the United States for India in the first nine months of 2026, The American Bazaar reported, citing Xpheno data first published by The Economic Times. At the current pace, the full-year figure will pass the 15,100 recorded in 2025 — itself a record.

"At the current pace, the full-year figure will pass the 15,100 recorded in 2025 — itself a record."

A flow that runs in both directions

The Xpheno counts are staffing-industry estimates built from the firm's candidate database, recruitment systems and job boards, not an official government tally of departures, and they cover the whole white-collar tech corridor rather than H-1B holders alone. Movement also continues in the other direction: Hind Himalaya reported that The People's Board estimated nearly 14,500 technology professionals moved from India to the US through September, so arrivals still exceed returns. What has changed is the direction of the trend line — returns have nearly doubled in three years while the policy environment for staying has tightened on several fronts at once.

Why professionals are leaving

The sharpest new pressure is on the green-card pipeline. PERM — Program Electronic Review Management — is the labour-certification step in which an employer must show that no qualified US worker is available for a job before sponsoring a foreign employee for permanent residence. PERM processing has been suspended for some of the largest recruiters of global talent, among them Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Cognizant, Capgemini, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Tata. Immigration expert Swatilina Barik noted that the suspension does not cancel existing H-1B visas or green cards already approved; it blocks new PERM filings and pauses pending ones, stalling the permanent-residency path for employees at those firms while leaving their temporary work authorisation intact.

Layered on top are wider signals of a tougher regime — the proposed end of deference to prior petition approvals, which would raise scrutiny at every extension (we covered the proposal here), and the H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act, introduced on October 1 by Republican Representative Beth Van Duyne of Texas, which would raise penalties for employers that intentionally break H-1B rules to fines of up to $250,000 and bans from federal and immigration programmes of up to 10 years. For professionals weighing a decade-long green-card queue against that backdrop, an India offer with family support nearby has become an easier calculation.

The landing is not guaranteed

Returnees are arriving in an Indian market that is hiring selectively, not booming. As LinkedIn commentator Abhinarayan Mishra pointed out, coming home does not guarantee an "easy landing": employers and global capability centres are paying a premium for artificial intelligence, cloud computing, cybersecurity and product leadership, and discounting general international experience that used to command a markup on its own. Returnees also carry practical baggage — tax compliance in both the US and India during the transition, and schooling and adjustment questions for children who have grown up in the US system.

What to watch

The fourth quarter will show whether 2026 clears the 15,100 mark and by how much. The bigger question is composition: if the outflow is concentrated among mid-career professionals stalled in the green-card queue, US employers lose exactly the experienced cohort their India capability centres are now competing to hire — and the corridor's centre of gravity shifts a little further toward Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune with every quarter like this one.
